summary: AstroVital is a health-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions like a 900-day Mars trip. It runs entirely on board and works without a link to Earth. It brings together wearable vitals, NASA space-weather data and machine-learning models trained on public datasets (heart-rhythm ECG, stress, sleep, bone loss and solar-storm forecasting). From these it gives each crew member a live risk score and the next steps to take, so the crew and their medical officer can act early without waiting on mission control. Simulators let teams rehearse emergencies before they happen: a mission clock that runs from day 1 to day 900, a spacecraft damage simulator and a 3D physics game with real emergency drills.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
AstroVital is a crew health-monitoring system for long missions, such as a roughly 900-day trip to Mars, where the communication delay with Earth can reach about 22 minutes each way. It brings together each astronaut’s vital signs, daily check-ins, cognitive tests, cabin conditions and space-weather data. Machine-learning models running on board turn this into a risk score from 0 to 100 for 11 health areas: radiation, heart, stress, sleep, bone loss, behavioral health, immune health, vision (SANS), cognitive performance, habitat exposure and drift from the astronaut’s personal baseline. Each risk comes with clear next steps taken from a fixed protocol library, so the system works fully offline with no language model. An optional language model only rewords the explanations.

The models are:

  • a solar-storm forecaster trained on NASA DONKI space-weather records
  • a neural network that detects abnormal heart rhythms, trained on the MIT-BIH ECG dataset
  • a stress classifier trained on WESAD
  • a sleep-stage model trained on Sleep-EDF
  • a bone-density model based on NHANES data
  • an Isolation Forest that learns each astronaut’s normal baseline and flags unusual changes

Benefits

  • Problems are caught early, without waiting for mission control.
    • a mission clock that plays the whole mission from day 1 to day 900
    • a What-if Lab for changing conditions and seeing the effect
    • a spacecraft damage simulator that handles several failures at once
    • an ECG lab
    • a 3D emergency-drill game (hull breach, fire, CO₂ scrubber failure, solar storm, ammonia leak) that ends by showing the real response protocol

Intended impact
To give crews more independence over their own medical decisions on missions where Earth can’t respond in time. To reduce preventable health risks such as radiation overexposure, bone loss, sleep problems and stress. To keep crews ready for emergencies through regular practice. The same approach could also be used in remote places on Earth, such as Antarctic stations, submarines and rural clinics.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Frontend: React 18 (JavaScript/JSX), Vite, React Router, Framer Motion, Recharts, three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, Rapier physics, Lucide icons
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite
  • Machine learning: scikit-learn, ONNX Runtime, NumPy
  • Data and APIs: NASA Open APIs (DONKI space weather), USDA FoodData Central (nutrition), and the public datasets MIT-BIH, WESAD, Sleep-EDF and NHANES
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Hardware: designed to take data from wearable sensors (ECG and heart rate, SpO₂, sleep tracking, a personal radiation dosimeter) and cabin CO₂ sensors. The current demo uses simulated sensor data.

How it is creative

  • It combines many separate health signals into one prediction for each astronaut, instead of showing isolated readings.
  • An interactive storyline explains the real health risks of spaceflight using NASA references.
  • Training is turned into a game with XP, ranks, badges and daily missions, which encourages crews to keep doing check-ins and drills.
  • The 3D physics drills run at Mars gravity, so emergency practice is hands-on rather than a checklist.

What the team considered

  • No dependence on Earth: everything runs on board, with no constant connection needed.
  • Explainable and safe: alerts follow fixed protocols, and the language model is optional.
  • Only real public datasets and real NASA references were used.
  • Personal baselines, because what is normal differs from one astronaut to another.
  • Fast to read under stress, with accessibility built in: keyboard navigation, readable contrast and support for reduced motion.
  • Privacy: health data stays on the spacecraft.
  • Low computing cost, so it can run on flight hardware.
